# Custom closet brand: separating the company from its first showroom

A custom closet and wardrobe company with showrooms in several states ran everything from one website. Search engines kept merging the brand with its original showroom, and its location pages, Google Business Profiles, and town pages stepped on each other.

## The engagement

A fixed-price project in milestones, delivering recommendations and structured data ready for the developer to install.

## What I delivered

### A clear entity model

The company described as the parent organization, and each showroom as a branch of it, so search engines and AI assistants can tell which is the brand and which is one of its locations. The JSON-LD states that relationship explicitly.

### Organization and product markup

Home page and product JSON-LD, validated and ready to install.

### Location pages matched to profiles

Each Google Business Profile linking to a page about that specific showroom, rather than to the home page.

### Profiles and town pages with separate jobs

Guidance for areas where a profile and a town page cover the same ground, so they reinforce each other.

### Services, regions, and breadcrumbs

A structure for how services, regions, and showrooms link together, reflected in breadcrumb markup.

## Why it matters

When every page and listing describes the business the same way, search engines can't tell the locations apart, and each one competes with the others. Distinct entities and distinct pages let every showroom rank in its own area while the brand ranks for itself.

## Status

Delivered. See [schema markup and entity SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/schema/) and [local SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/).

Updated: 2026-10-06

# Therapy practice: a suspended Business Profile restored

Google suspended the Business Profile of a hypnotherapy office in western Canada. The practice depends on nearby people finding it, so the suspension left it close to invisible to the very clients most likely to book.

## My part

Auditing the listing against the office's real records, assembling proof, writing the appeal, and seeing it through with Google.

## Reconcile the listing with reality

Google suspends a listing when what it claims can't be squared with what Google is able to confirm. So I went field by field: the practice's legal and trading names, its street address, its categories, and whether it served clients on site. Anything on the listing that didn't match the paperwork was corrected before a word of the appeal was written.

## Lead with the best proof

The supporting file contained the office lease, the practice's business licence, an invoice billed to that office, and the business card carrying the same name and address. I ordered them from most to least authoritative, so a reviewer would see the strongest proof first, and the appeal made no claim that one of those documents didn't back up.

## File the appeal

The corrected listing and the ordered proof reached Google as one package, so the reviewer saw the fixes and the evidence side by side.

## Result

Google restored the profile in February 2025.

## How I handle these now

Google gives no timetable and no guarantee for appeals, and two cases that look alike can end differently. For that reason a suspension now starts with a paid written assessment: the likely trigger, the proof Google will expect, and an honest view of the odds. If an appeal makes sense, it's quoted on its own. I take the same approach with harder situations, like duplicate records, listings stranded with a former agency, or an established listing that should be repaired rather than replaced. See [local SEO and Google Business Profile](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/).

# AI research company: accurate AI answers for job seekers

An AI research company was hiring engineers in Palo Alto and across the Bay Area. Engineers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google's AI features who's hiring and what they pay, so the company wanted to know how it showed up in those answers.

## The engagement

A defined AI search visibility audit with recommendations.

## What I examined
- Whether, and how, the company appeared when assistants were asked the questions engineers ask about jobs, employers, and compensation.
- Which sources those answers relied on, and where the company's own information was absent or outweighed.
- How consistently the company's name, description, and relationship to its related domains were stated across the web.
- Careers content across two company domains.

## What I recommended
- Careers pages and FAQs rewritten around candidates' actual questions.
- Metadata and structured data for careers and company pages.
- Compensation facts drawn from the company's approved figures, stated clearly enough for assistants to quote correctly.
- Third-party references worth pursuing, since assistants treat outside sources as corroboration.

## Why it's a useful example

Nothing here was about selling a product. The goal was to be described accurately to a specific audience making an important decision. The same audit applies wherever people consult an assistant before acting: choosing a vendor, an employer, an investment, or a professional.

## What carries over

Careers questions are a clean test of AI visibility because the facts are specific and checkable: locations, roles, pay ranges, and benefits.

## Status

Recommendations delivered; the engagement is paused. See [AI SEO, GEO, and AEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/ai-search/) or the [AI search readiness checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-search-checklist/).

# About Christopher Abraham

I'm an independent SEO consultant in Arlington, Virginia, across the Potomac from Washington, DC. I've called the DC area home since college, and I take clients across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand.

## What I'm working on now
- Testing how AI assistants describe businesses and people, and fixing what they get wrong.
- Finding content that JavaScript frameworks hide from crawlers, on React, Next.js, Alpine.js, and headless builds.
- Making SEO changes through pull requests on GitHub, alongside the developers who own the code.
- Reading repositories with AI coding assistants to plan migrations before anything breaks.
- Writing structured data that ties organizations, locations, and people together as entities.

## How I got here

My first online home was a text-based conferencing system, and I've kept an account on The WELL, one of the oldest online communities, for decades. That's where my email address comes from. I built my first websites in 1994, hand-coding HTML for anyone who asked, and started optimizing them for search engines in 1998. I've worked with open-source content management systems since 1999: Movable Type, Plone, Drupal, WordPress, and plenty of platforms that no longer exist.

Before the agencies, I was an associate at Rheingold Associates, the virtual community consultancy of Howard Rheingold, a Linux system administrator at Caucus Systems running professional online events, and a builder of websites for clients that included the Treasury Department.

In the agency years I was the technology strategist at New Media Strategies, one of the first firms to treat a brand's online reputation as something to manage, and then a senior account supervisor on the interactive team at Edelman's public affairs practice in Washington. In 2006 I developed long-tail blogger outreach: rather than pitching a handful of famous bloggers, my team researched and pitched thousands of niche writers who actually cared about a client's subject, treating it as earned media, closer to public relations than to paid social. I co-founded Abraham Harrison, a digital marketing firm that ran search, content, and outreach programs from Washington, Portland, and Berlin. It ran as a fully virtual company before that was normal: two founders and fourteen contractors across the United States, Europe, India, and Africa, spread over ten time zones. Google liked the setup enough to publish [a case study about the firm](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/www.google.com/en//a/help/intl/en/admins/case_studies/pdf/abraham_harrison_cs.pdf), quoting me as president and COO. Later I was team lead for special projects at Reputation.com, working with high-profile individuals on search results that mattered to them.

A word about New Media Strategies, because it shaped everything after. I was employee number 13 there, from 2002 to 2006, in an open-plan former newsroom in a Rosslyn tower, back when word-of-mouth marketing meant joining online communities and becoming a real, contributing member of them for months before a client's name ever came up. The firm grew past 120 people and trained every new hire, me included, as if it were a discretion bootcamp. In 2002 I helped develop the practice that became online reputation management, which I've done in one form or another ever since. I've written the whole story up, tongue firmly in cheek, as ["I was a teenage Russian troll."](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/i-teenage-russian-troll-chris-abraham) I was neither a teenager nor Russian. And yes, working under a nom de guerre is an old habit.

I'm proud to work alongside two firms: as a digital strategist with [Meritus Media](https://meritusmedia.com/), a digital PR and marketing agency, where search, Google Business Profile, and reputation work sit beside the PR, and as a business partner at [Stainless Communications](https://stainlesscommunications.com/), a senior-led brand, PR, web, and growth firm.

My independent practice runs mostly through Upwork and centers on the technical end of search: why a page isn't indexed, why a template hides content from the crawler, why a migration lost traffic, and how a business shows up when someone asks an AI assistant about it.

## What I'm known for
- **Forensics.** I like the cases nobody else could explain. The answer is usually a mechanism: a script that never runs for Googlebot, a canonical pointing at the wrong page, a redirect chain that drops equity at every hop.

# Off the clock

Clients hire me to read crawl data, but it helps to know the fellow reading it. I've been curious about nearly everything for as long as I can remember, and I've never been very good at picking just one thing. Here's the rest of the story, told plainly and with as little bragging as I can manage.

## A Honolulu boyhood

I grew up in Honolulu, in Salt Lake, the neighborhood next to the airport (not the one in Utah, whatever the AI summaries say). I went to Aliamanu Elementary, right there in the neighborhood, from kindergarten through sixth grade, then to Saint Louis School for seventh through twelfth grade, where I somehow ended up student body president while also doing JROTC, the Ranger Club, wrestling, the newspaper, the yearbook, the photography club, and the Bullseye Club. I ran out of high school courses before I ran out of high school, so I took philosophy classes at Chaminade University, which shared the school's campus.

My father was a photographer, and my mother had traveled through Europe and the United States before I came along, so hopping on a plane was simply normal in the Abraham household. Once, when an eruption was announced, my dad pulled me out of elementary school to fly to the Big Island and see it. Tramping around on lava flows at nine years old makes a lasting impression on a kid.

## College, crew, and a year abroad

Washington got me first through Close Up, a summer program on politics for high school students. Then a GW catalog arrived at home in Honolulu with a photo of the crew rowing across a glassy, misty Potomac at dawn, and that was that. I came to Washington for The George Washington University. I started in political science, switched to American literature, and minored in creative writing; I'm told mine was one of the last American literature degrees GW ever granted. I'd never rowed a stroke, but I'd seen Oxford Blues in high school, so naturally I rowed heavyweight crew, was a founding father of the Phi Kappa Psi chapter on campus, hosted a weekly house music and comedy show on WRGW radio, interned in the Washington bureau of The Baltimore Sun, and edited the English department's newsletter.

My adviser, the English professor Robert Combs, steered me toward a year abroad, so midway through I spent a year at the University of East Anglia in Norwich, England, reading postwar American literature. I rowed for UEA too, worked the door as a bouncer at the student nightclub, spent weekends in Paris whenever the budget allowed, and once left class for two weeks to trek the Kathmandu Valley. Then I took a year off before my senior year and went home to Honolulu to work as a commercial photographer, studying French at the University of Hawaiʻi on the side. Later I sold my work as a stock photographer through an agency in New York.

GW Today, the university's news site, once [wrote up some of this story](https://gwtoday.gwu.edu/marketing-online-and-around-world), and I'll admit I still think of old buff and blue every time I get all the cartoons in The New Yorker.

## Languages, mostly attempted

French in Hawaii, German at the Goethe-Institut in Washington and again in Berlin. My German is solidly A2, which is enough to order lunch with confidence and apologize for it fluently. Abraham Harrison, the firm I co-founded, ran for a time from Washington, Portland, and Berlin, so the lessons got real use.

## Online before it was a career

Back when getting online meant a modem and patience, I joined ArtsWire, then The Meta Network, one of Washington's first online communities, then Brainstorms, and The WELL, where I've kept a home ever since; that's why my email ends in well.com. My first real mentor online was [Frank Burns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_L._Burns), who founded The Meta Network: a retired Army lieutenant colonel with a Silver Star from Vietnam, widely credited with the "Be All That You Can Be" slogan, who spent his retirement building tools for people to think together online. He ran Metasystems Design Group, the makers of the Caucus conferencing software, and I later worked in a support role on his New MetaNet. Frank was a friend as much as a teacher, and a good deal of what I believe about online community I learned from him.

I built websites by hand for anyone who'd let me, including sites for a consulting firm, a production company, the Shadow Conventions, and the Treasury Department, and I worked as a Linux system administrator at Caucus Systems, hosting professional virtual events on its conferencing software.

I also co-taught, with Ginny Little, one of the first fully accredited online high school courses: creative writing for EFA, a magnet program of the Kalamazoo Public Schools in Michigan, with more than sixty students logging in from around the area. The lesson I took from it, and later wrote a column about, is that children naturally want to show what they know. And I became an associate of Howard Rheingold, the author of The Virtual Community, at Rheingold Associates; [my old team bio is still up](https://rheingold.com/Associates/team_abraham.html), which delights me more than it should.

I published a memetic lexicon at Memes.org, founded MemeSpace, a free online community of more than 800 "memebers" that The New York Times once wrote about, and ran a little online publication called The Caffeinated Magazine. These days I'm the founding moderator of [r/slowjogging](https://www.reddit.com/r/slowjogging/), a Reddit community of more than 16,000 people practicing the gentle, smile-while-you-run method of the late Japanese exercise physiologist Hiroaki Tanaka. After nine years it still has nothing to sell: no coaching funnel, no membership tier, no merchandise. Watching ideas spread and mutate online for as long as I have turns out to be excellent training for understanding how AI assistants pick up and repeat what they read.

>

"I met Chris … as part of my work for Arts Wire, an online network for artists. He was an early adopter of the Web and has context."

Beth Kanter, master trainer and nonprofit innovator in networks, learning, and social media

## Hyperfiction

Before anybody called it electronic literature, I was writing it. I was one of the eight writers of Name is Scibe, a collaborative hyperfiction that Judy Malloy, one of the true pioneers of the form, began on Arts Wire and The WELL. [Her own history of the piece](http://www.judymalloy.net/intaud.html) lists the writers, and [The WELL still hosts the original text](https://people.well.com/user/jmalloy/scibe/), my entries included. Then I led my own: 8: A Collaborative Hypernarrative Fiction, or Collabor8, written over a full year by a group of friends, with each story broken into linked fragments that readers wandered through in their own order. Pieces of it survive as found poems with titles like "Chocolate City," "TheBUS," and "Blue plastic kayaks." Afterward I started Coelaboration, a site for collaborative writing with a featured writer each month and the beginnings of yet another hypernarrative.

It turns out that writing stories as a web of linked pages is decent preparation for a career thinking about how crawlers move through websites.

## Lodge, rite, and parish

I'm a Master Mason at Naval Lodge No. 4 on Capitol Hill, the oldest continuously operating lodge in the District of Columbia, first chartered in 1805. I'm also a 32nd degree Scottish Rite Mason in the Southern Jurisdiction, whose headquarters, the House of the Temple, sits on 16th Street in Washington. Before that I served on the vestry of St. Monica and St. James, an Episcopal parish on Capitol Hill, and, naturally, I ended up as its webmaster too.

## Renaissance Weekend

I've been a member of Renaissance Weekend for many years, though I haven't made it to one in a while: invitation-only, off-the-record gatherings where a physicist, a poet, a senator, and a teenager might share a panel. I've moderated sessions and worn the blue dot. It's the closest thing I know to a polymath's playground, and it's taught me that the best ideas come from people outside your own field.

At one Renaissance Weekend I shared a panel with Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, the two engineers who designed the internet's core protocols. Just those two and me. At others I spent a lot of happy hours with Esther Dyson, the investor and early internet thinker who trained as a backup cosmonaut, in her trademark jeans.

## Miriam's Kitchen

For years I volunteered as a sous chef at Miriam's Kitchen, which works to end chronic homelessness in Washington. Cooking for guests who deserved a good meal was the most useful work I did all week, nobody in that kitchen cared about my rankings, and I hope to be back at the cutting board one day.

## On the water and on the road

I was a senior member of the Potomac Boat Club, founded in 1869 and one of the oldest rowing clubs in the country, and I may well be again someday. For years I kept my own racing shell, a heavyweight Hudson carbon single, at Thompson Boat Center, and I eventually gave it to the club to join its fleet of training singles, where it can teach somebody else what Oxford Blues taught me. On land I'm a slow jogger, which is exactly as fast as it sounds. If I'm honest, these days it's not enough jogging and plenty of modding.

## Teaching and talking

I've been a guest lecturer at Georgetown, GW, American University, the University of Maryland, the University of Oregon, and Columbia, and I taught blogging and early SEO at The Writer's Center in Bethesda. I've been called on by BBC World Service and CNN Radio to talk about technology and the internet, and I spoke on a panel at South by Southwest.

## Why any of this matters to you

I spent a good part of my career on the bleeding edge: online events before anyone had heard of webinars, hyperfiction before e-lit had a name, memes before they were jokes, reputation management before it was an industry. These days I'm happy on the bleedy edge, early enough to put new tools to work for clients and seasoned enough to know which ones have earned it.

A polymath is a big word for a modest man, so I'll settle for generalist with a specialty. Literature taught me to read closely, photography taught me to notice what's in the frame and what isn't, rowing taught me that nothing moves unless everyone pulls together, and the lodge taught me patience with ritual and process. All of it shows up when I'm looking at your site. Back to the [work side of my story](https://christopherabraham.com/about/), or [say hello](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

# How these pages are written and checked

Everything on this site is published by me, Christopher Abraham, and I'm responsible for every word of it. Here's how the guides, case studies, and service pages are made, so you can decide how much to trust them.

## Written from the work

The case studies describe engagements I worked on myself: the problem, my role, what I found, what was done and by whom, and where it stands. The guides come from the same work. When I explain how to read the Page indexing report or how to lock down a domain that sends no email, it's because I've done it for clients or for my own sites, often in the same week.

## Primary sources for every factual claim

Where a guide states how Google, Bing, a standard, or a protocol behaves, it links to the primary documentation: Google Search Central, Bing Webmaster Guidelines, the W3C's accessibility standards, the RFCs that define email records, and the specifications for files like llms.txt. Those links are listed under "Sources" at the end of each guide, and in the page's structured data as citations. When the official documentation and common practice disagree, I say so.

## How I use AI tools

I use AI assistants the way I'd use a capable junior colleague: to draft outlines and first passes, to check code and markup, and to build and test this site's generator. I don't publish anything they produce until I've read it, corrected it, and checked its claims. Two rules are absolute:
- **Personal and biographical details come only from my own records** and verifiable published sources, never from an AI summary. AI search tools have confidently told the world things about me that aren't true, and none of those get a second life here.
- **Technical claims are checked against primary documentation**, not against what an assistant remembers.

## Clients and confidentiality

Case studies describe clients by industry and problem, never by name, and leave out anything that could identify them: addresses, revenue, account details, and screenshots of private dashboards. Where a client's engagement is ongoing or paused, the case study says so. I don't claim results I can't show, and I don't round up.

## Quotes and testimonials

Quotes from clients and colleagues are reproduced as written, with attribution. Where I've shortened a quote, an ellipsis marks the cut. Upwork figures, such as my Job Success Score and job counts, are copied from my profile with the date they were taken, and the profile itself is linked so anyone can check the current numbers.

## Independence
- No affiliate links, sponsored posts, or paid placements, anywhere on the site.
- Tools and platforms are named because I use them or because clients run on them, not because anyone pays me to mention them.
- The firms I'm affiliated with are named on the About page, so you can weigh any recommendation with that in mind.

## Dates and updates

Every guide shows when it was published and when it was last updated. Search changes quickly, so I revise guides when Google, Bing, or a standard changes, and the updated date moves with the revision. Pages describing my own memberships and activities use past and present tense carefully, and I correct them when something changes.

## Corrections

If you find an error, email [cja@well.com](mailto:cja@well.com) with the page and what's wrong. I'll check it against the source, fix it if you're right, and update the page's date. Significant corrections to a guide are noted on the guide itself.

## Who's behind the site

This is a one-person practice. My background, credentials, and the third-party sources that confirm them are on the [About page](https://christopherabraham.com/about/), and the life behind the work is [off the clock](https://christopherabraham.com/about/off-the-clock/). You can also find me on [Upwork](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/chrisjabraham) and [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chrisabraham), or [get in touch directly](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

# Hire me

Every engagement follows the same arc: a defined question, a paid audit that answers it, a ranked plan, the fixes, and a verification pass once the fixes are live. Here's how each step works and what I need from you.

## Two ways to hire me
- **On Upwork.** Most of my clients hire me through [my Upwork profile](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/chrisjabraham). Upwork handles contracts, time tracking, invoicing, and payment protection for both sides. Hourly and fixed-price contracts both work there.
- **Directly.** Email [cja@well.com](mailto:cja@well.com) and I'll send a written scope and an invoice. Direct engagements are paid in advance: the audit up front, retainers at the start of each month.

## The process
1. **A short conversation.** You tell me the symptom; I ask what changed, when, and who has access to what. A few emails or a [30 minute call](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30) is usually enough.
2. **A written scope.** The questions the audit will answer, what you'll receive, the access I'll need, the timeline, and the price.
3. **The audit.** Crawls, Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools data, rendered HTML, server responses, and whatever else the question calls for. You receive a findings report with the cause, the evidence, and a ranked list of fixes.
4. **The fixes.** I make the changes I have access to, such as metadata, redirects, schema, plugin settings, and Cloudflare rules. For everything that needs a developer, I write tickets with steps and acceptance criteria.
5. **Verification.** Once changes ship, I check the live site, request recrawls where they help, and watch the reports until the trend is clear.

## What I need from you
- Access to Google Search Console and, if you have it, Bing Webmaster Tools. Full user access is ideal; I'll explain why when it matters.
- Read access to analytics, usually GA4.
- A content management login with a role that fits the work, or a staging copy.
- An introduction to whoever deploys code, if that isn't you.
- A named person who answers questions and approves changes.

## Where the work lives

I keep every engagement in writing: Upwork messages, email, or your project tool, whether that's Basecamp, Asana, Jira, or a shared Google Drive folder. Calls are welcome for kickoff and walkthroughs, and each call gets a written follow-up so decisions survive. A written record makes the work easier to review, easier to hand to a developer, and easier to pick up six months later.

## Pricing

I quote hourly or a fixed price per milestone, whichever fits the job. Audits are scoped and priced before they start, so you know the cost of an answer before you commit to it. Retainers cover a set number of hours each month with a monthly report. My current hourly rate is on [my Upwork profile](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/chrisjabraham).

## What I sell, and what nobody can

I sell expertise, diagnosis, and hands-on work. Rankings, indexing decisions, AI answers, and Google Business Profile reviews belong to the platforms, and each one decides on its own schedule. So I commit to the work and the evidence, and I report honestly on what the platforms do in response.

Questions about time zones, access, and invoicing are answered in the [FAQ](https://christopherabraham.com/faq/). Ready to start? Head to [contact](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

# Frequently asked questions

Practical answers about how an engagement runs. For the overall process, see [Hire Me](https://christopherabraham.com/hire-me/).

### How long does an SEO audit take?

Most audits take one to two weeks from the day I have access. Large sites, sites with many subdomains, or questions that need server logs take longer, and the scope states the timeline up front.

### What do I receive at the end of an audit?

A written findings report: the question, what I examined, what I found, the evidence for each finding, and a prioritized list of fixes with an owner for each one. Developer items come as tickets with acceptance criteria. I walk you through it on a call if you'd like.

### Do I have to hire you through Upwork?

No. Upwork is convenient for many clients because it handles contracts and payments, and that's where my reviews live. You can also hire me directly by email, with payment in advance.

### What access will you need?

Usually Google Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools, GA4, and a login for your content management system. For JavaScript and headless sites, read access to the code repository helps a great deal. I'll list exactly what's needed in the scope.

### Will you change things on my live site?

Only with your approval, and only changes that are in scope. Theme and template work happens on a staging site or a duplicate theme first. Every change I make is logged so you can see what moved and when.

### Can you work with my developer?

Yes, and I prefer it. I write specifications developers can build from, review pull requests when I have repository access, and verify the live result after deployment.

### What time zone do you work in?

US Eastern time. I schedule calls across North America, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand, and most of the work happens in writing, so time zones rarely slow a project down.

### How soon will I see results?

Technical fixes can show up in crawl data within days. Indexing changes usually take weeks, and ranking and AI answer changes can take months. I set expectations for each item in the plan and report on them as they move.

### Do you write content?

I write and edit metadata, FAQs, page outlines, and service page copy as part of SEO work, using AI tools for drafts and my own editing for the final version. For a full content program, I can brief and edit your writers.

### Do you offer monthly SEO?

Yes. A [retainer](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-retainer/) covers monitoring, fixes, and reporting each month, billed at the start of the month.

### How do you handle confidential information?

Client details stay private. Case studies on this site describe clients by industry and problem, never by name. I'm happy to sign a nondisclosure agreement, and I've worked under HIPAA terms on a healthcare site.

Something else? Email [cja@well.com](mailto:cja@well.com).

# Privacy

This site runs one script: Google Analytics 4, which tells me roughly how many people visit, which pages they read, and how they found the site. It runs no advertising, no remarketing, and no other tracking.

## Analytics, in detail
- **Advertising features are off for everyone.** Ad storage, ad user data, and ad personalization are all switched off in the site's consent settings, so visits here are never used to target ads.
- **Visitors in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom** get no analytics cookies at all. Google receives only cookieless, aggregate signals from those regions.
- **Visitors elsewhere** get first-party Google Analytics cookies, named `_ga` and `_ga_` followed by an ID, that tell repeat visits apart from new ones. They hold a random identifier, not your name or email.
- Google processes the data under its own privacy policy. I see aggregate reports: page views, rough location by country or city, device type, and referring sites, including AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Perplexity.

To opt out on every site that uses Google Analytics, install Google's opt-out browser add-on, or block cookies for this site in your browser settings. Everything here works the same with analytics blocked.

## What the host sees

GitHub Pages serves the site. GitHub's servers receive the connecting IP address and the requested page, as every web host does, and may retain those logs for security under GitHub's privacy statement. I can't see them.

## Everything else on the page

Pages, images, and styles all load from this domain. There are no embedded videos, social buttons, third-party fonts, or pixels. Outbound links, such as those to Upwork and Calendly, lead to sites with their own policies.

## Messages and calls

An email, call, or text gives me your address or number and whatever you write. I use it to answer you and, if you hire me, to do the work. It's never sold, shared for marketing, or added to a list. Logins and analytics access granted during an engagement serve that engagement only, and I give them up when it ends or whenever you ask.

## Crawlers

Search engines and AI crawlers may read and cite the public pages, as described in [robots.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/robots.txt). No visitor information goes to them.

## Questions

Write to [cja@well.com](mailto:cja@well.com) with any privacy question, or to have me delete your past emails with me.

# Site map

Every page on this site, grouped by section, with a one-line summary of each. Search engines read the same list in [sitemap.xml](https://christopherabraham.com/sitemap.xml), and AI tools in [llms.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/llms.txt).

## Main pages
- [Senior SEO help, from the person who does the work](https://christopherabraham.com/): Christopher Abraham is a senior SEO consultant: technical audits, indexing repair, schema, site speed, migrations, and visibility in AI answer engines.
- [SEO services](https://christopherabraham.com/services/): Thirteen SEO services: audits, indexing repair, JavaScript SEO, site speed, migrations, schema, AI search, WordPress, ecommerce, local SEO, and retainers.
- [SEO guides](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/): Practical SEO guides: reading the Page indexing report, AI search readiness, judging audits, small business schema, 301 redirects, and Core Web Vitals.
- [Case studies](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/): Anonymized SEO case studies: hidden product content, consent tools blocking Google, React apps, migrations, programmatic indexing, schema, and local listings.
- [About Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/): Christopher Abraham is an SEO consultant in Arlington, VA, working on AI search, rendering forensics, and modern stacks, with SEO experience dating to 1998.
- [Hire me](https://christopherabraham.com/hire-me/): How an SEO engagement runs: a scoped, paid audit first, then hourly or fixed price work through Upwork or direct, with every finding and decision in writing.
- [Frequently asked questions](https://christopherabraham.com/faq/): Practical answers about an SEO engagement: what access is needed, how long audits take, time zones, Upwork contracts, invoicing, reports, and confidentiality.
- [Contact Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/): Email Christopher Abraham at cja@well.com or call or text him with your site address and the problem. Hire him on Upwork or directly for a scoped audit.
- [Privacy](https://christopherabraham.com/privacy/): How christopherabraham.com uses Google Analytics with consent mode, why visitors in Europe and the UK get no analytics cookies, and what happens to your email.

## Technical SEO
- [Technical SEO audit](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-audit/): A technical SEO audit that answers one question with evidence: why traffic fell or stalled, the mechanism behind it, and which fixes should come first.
- [Indexing repair](https://christopherabraham.com/services/indexing/): Fix Google indexing problems: pages crawled but not indexed, discovered but never crawled, soft 404s, canonical conflicts, and sitemaps that mislead.
- [JavaScript and headless SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/javascript-seo/): Make JavaScript and headless websites visible to search and AI crawlers: rendering comparisons, crawlable links, prerendering, and code level review.
- [Core Web Vitals and Cloudflare](https://christopherabraham.com/services/site-speed/): Speed up a website for real visitors: Core Web Vitals diagnosis, image and script cleanup, page caching, and Cloudflare rules that still welcome crawlers.
- [Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools, and GA4](https://christopherabraham.com/services/search-console/): Set up and clean up Google Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools, and GA4 so every report is verified, accurate, owned by you, and useful for decisions.
- [Site migrations and 301 redirects](https://christopherabraham.com/services/migrations/): Plan and verify a website migration: full URL inventories, one to one 301 redirect maps, launch day checks, and recovery when a move has already lost traffic.

## AI search, schema, and content
- [AI SEO, GEO, and AEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/ai-search/): Improve how ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, and Google AI Overviews describe and cite your business, with prompt testing, entities, and content.
- [Schema markup and entity SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/schema/): Structured data that validates, matches the visible page, and connects your organization, people, products, and locations as entities for Google and AI.
- [On-page SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/on-page-seo/): On page SEO fixed at the template level: titles and meta descriptions, headings, internal links, thin and duplicate pages, and carefully edited AI drafts.

## Platforms, local, and ongoing work
- [WordPress SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/wordpress-seo/): WordPress SEO done carefully: Yoast and Rank Math settings, theme and plugin conflicts, page builder bloat, caching, and old installs that need a steady hand.
- [Ecommerce SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/ecommerce-seo/): Ecommerce SEO for Shopify, WooCommerce, and Magento: product and category templates, faceted navigation, duplicate URLs, product schema, and AI answers.
- [Local SEO and Google Business Profile](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/): Align your website, location pages, and Google Business Profiles, with hard profile cases like suspensions handled as scoped, paid written diagnostics.
- [Monthly SEO retainer](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-retainer/): A monthly SEO retainer with a senior consultant: monitoring, hands on fixes, developer QA, AI search checks, and a plain English report every month.

## Guides
- [How to read the Page indexing report in Search Console](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/page-indexing-report/): A field guide to Search Console's Page indexing report: what each exclusion reason means, which ones need action, and how to find the template behind them.
- [The AI search readiness checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-search-checklist/): A practical checklist for AI search: crawler access, server rendered content, entity schema, answer shaped pages, llms.txt, outside evidence, and measurement.
- [What a technical SEO audit should give you](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/seo-audit-deliverables/): How to tell a useful technical SEO audit from a tool export: a clear question, evidence for each finding, a ranked plan, developer tickets, and a plain summary.
- [The schema markup a small business actually needs](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/small-business-schema/): Which schema types a small business needs, which to skip, and example structured data for local businesses, services, FAQs, and breadcrumbs, kept accurate.
- [Ten rules for 301 redirects that keep your rankings](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/redirect-rules/): Ten rules for 301 redirects in migrations and redesigns: map one to one, avoid chains, keep redirects for years, use 410 on purpose, and test in bulk.
- [Core Web Vitals in plain English](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/core-web-vitals/): Core Web Vitals explained without jargon: what LCP, INP, and CLS measure, why lab scores differ from field data, the usual causes, and the fixes that work.
- [How to correct what AI search says about you](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/correct-ai-answers/): When ChatGPT, Gemini, or Google's AI Overviews get your facts wrong, here is how to find where the error came from and publish corrections that get picked up.
- [One person, two names: entity SEO for pen names and nicknames](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/two-names-one-entity/): How to make Google and AI assistants see that Christopher and Chris, or a pen name and a legal name, are one person, using schema, sameAs, and consistency.
- [Proving expertise with third-party sources](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/third-party-proof/): Your own claims carry little weight with Google and AI assistants. University news, vendor case studies, old bios, and bylines do. How to find and use them.
- [How to write an About page that search engines and AI trust](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/about-page-ai/): A recipe for an About page that Google and AI assistants quote correctly: current work first, verifiable facts, outside sources, schema, and no guesswork.
- [Launch a site on a parked domain with Cloudflare and GitHub Pages](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/parked-domain-launch/): Step by step: take a domain off a parking page, move DNS to Cloudflare, point it at GitHub Pages, get HTTPS, and avoid the caching traps on launch day.
- [How to lock down a domain that never sends email](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/non-sending-domain/): Four DNS records stop spammers from forging mail from a domain you never send from: a null MX, an SPF that allows nothing, strict DMARC, and an empty DKIM key.
- [What happens to your old domains when they lapse](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/lapsed-domains/): When an old company or project domain expires, drop catchers buy it for its links and reputation. What they do with it, the harm, and how to protect yourself.
- [How to write an llms.txt file](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/llms-txt/): What llms.txt is, who reads it, and how to write one: the format, the full text companion file, Markdown page copies, robots.txt rules, and common mistakes.
- [Meta keywords in 2026: ignored, mostly harmless, used honestly](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/meta-keywords/): Google ignores the meta keywords tag and Bing has called stuffing it a spam signal. Why some sites still use it, and how to write one that does no harm at all.
- [Website accessibility without overlays](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/accessible-websites/): Build accessibility into a small business website instead of bolting on an overlay: contrast, headings, links, images, keyboard use, forms, and testing it.
- [Glossary of SEO and AI search terms](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/glossary/): Plain English definitions of SEO and AI search terms: AEO, GEO, canonical tags, crawl budget, entities, INP, IndexNow, llms.txt, soft 404s, and many more.

## Case studies
- [Equipment retailer: product details that loaded only on scroll](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/scroll-gated-products/): An equipment retailer on Magento and Hyvä lost organic traffic because Alpine.js loaded specs and reviews only on scroll. How the cause was isolated and proven.
- [Film review site: a consent tool that emptied every article for Google](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/consent-banner/): A bilingual film review site was indexed by Bing but nearly invisible in Google. A consent platform blocked the script that displayed every article to bots.
- [Event discovery app: 2,000 pages with no way in](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/event-app-links/): An event discovery app built with Create React App had 2,000 event pages Google never found. A 13 page spec, ranked P0 to P3, gave the developer exact fixes.
- [Junk removal company on a headless stack: SEO through the repository](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/headless-local/): A junk removal company on Sanity, Vercel, and GitHub had thin rendered HTML and duplicate metadata. Priorities set, a pull request merged, prerendering checked.
- [Medical clinic: WordPress to Next.js without losing the trail](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/clinic-migration/): SEO oversight for a clinic moving from WordPress to Next.js on Netlify: a decision for every legacy URL, an AI assisted code review, and a careful disavow.
- [Fly fishing shop: cleaning up after Squarespace to Shopify](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/shopify-cleanup/): A family owned fly fishing shop moved from Squarespace to Shopify and left 3,400 broken URLs and duplicate product paths. An audit and safe theme schema work.
- [Trading card price site: managing 20,000 pages in Google's index](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/card-price-index/): A trading card price site of more than 20,000 programmatic pages indexed well, then lost large sections of the index. How crawling is managed at that scale.
- [Health-testing store: recovering after the SEO plugin went dark](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/plugin-outage/): A WooCommerce store selling health tests lost indexing, traffic, and AI referrals when its SEO plugin was turned off. Diagnosis, fixes, and proof of recovery.
- [Custom closet brand: separating the company from its first showroom](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/closet-locations/): A custom closet company with showrooms in several states ran one website, and search engines blurred the brand with its first showroom. Entity and schema fixes.
- [Therapy practice: a suspended Business Profile restored](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/profile-reinstated/): A Canadian hypnotherapy office disappeared from Google Maps after a profile suspension. The listing was corrected, proof organized, and the profile restored.
- [AI research company: accurate AI answers for job seekers](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/recruiting-answers/): An AI research company hiring Bay Area engineers wanted ChatGPT and Perplexity to answer accurately about its jobs and pay. The audit findings and the plan.

## Files for machines
- [sitemap.xml](https://christopherabraham.com/sitemap.xml): the XML sitemap for search engines.
- [llms.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/llms.txt): a plain summary of the site for language models, linking to Markdown versions of every page.
- [llms-full.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/llms-full.txt): the full text of the site in one file.
- [feed.xml](https://christopherabraham.com/feed.xml) and [rss.xml](https://christopherabraham.com/rss.xml): Atom and RSS feeds of the guides.
- [llm.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/llm.txt): the same summary as llms.txt, at the other common address.
- [robots.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/robots.txt): crawler rules; every search engine and AI crawler is welcome.
